title: Ecological niches
summary: Each species has a niche: its role in the ecosystem. This topic covers oxygen requirements, modes of nutrition from photosynthesis to saprotrophy, and adaptations for feeding, defence and harvesting light. HL adds fundamental and realized niches and competitive exclusion.

keyterms.definition: The role of a species in an ecosystem, including its interactions with other species and its use of biotic and abiotic resources.
Organism that cannot use oxygen and is inhibited or killed by it, so lives only in anoxic environments.
Organism that respires aerobically when oxygen is available but can switch to anaerobic respiration without it, e.g. yeast.
Organism that requires a continuous supply of oxygen for aerobic respiration, e.g. humans.
Autotrophic nutrition using light energy to make organic compounds; found in plants, algae and several groups of prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria.
Heterotrophic nutrition in which food is ingested, digested internally, absorbed and assimilated; typical of animals.
Organism that can be both autotrophic and heterotrophic, e.g. Euglena, which photosynthesizes in light but can also feed on organic matter.
Organism that secretes digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbs the products (external digestion), e.g. many fungi and bacteria.
Archaea are diverse in nutrition: some use light energy, some oxidize inorganic chemicals (chemoautotrophs) and some oxidize organic compounds (heterotrophs).
Tooth structure reflects diet: e.g. large molars with thick enamel in herbivorous Paranthropus robustus; varied teeth in omnivorous Homo sapiens.
Herbivores have adaptations such as specialized mouthparts; plants resist them with physical defences (spines) and chemical defences (toxins).
Predators have adaptations for finding, catching and killing prey; prey have adaptations such as camouflage, warning colouration and toxins to resist predation.
Plant forms that gain light in forests: tall canopy trees, lianas climbing from the ground, epiphytes on branches and shade-tolerant shrubs.
The potential range of conditions and resources a species could occupy if there were no competition.
The actual range of conditions and resources a species occupies when competing with other species; usually smaller than the fundamental niche.
Principle that two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely: one will be eliminated or restricted to a smaller realized niche.

options: The physical place where an organism lives
The role of a species in its ecosystem, including its interactions and use of biotic and abiotic resources
The number of individuals of a species in an area
A group of ecosystems with similar climates
questions.explanation: A habitat is where a species lives; its niche is how it lives there: what it eats, what eats it, when it is active and which conditions and resources it uses.

questions.prompt: Match each type of organism to its relationship with oxygen.

pairs.right: Uses oxygen if available, respires anaerobically if not

questions.explanation: Oxygen requirements limit where organisms can live, so they are part of each species' niche.
Yeast respires aerobically when oxygen is present and switches to anaerobic respiration (producing ethanol and CO2) when it is not.

questions.text: Animals ingest food and digest it internally, a mode of nutrition called ___ nutrition.
questions.explanation: Holozoic nutrition involves taking food into the body before digesting it, unlike saprotrophs, which digest food outside their bodies.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of holozoic nutrition in order.
questions.explanation: Food is taken in, broken down by enzymes, absorbed into the body, built into the organism's own tissues, and undigested material is eliminated.

questions.prompt: How do saprotrophs obtain their nutrition?
options: By ingesting food and digesting it internally
By photosynthesis using chlorophyll
By living inside a host and taking its food
By secreting digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs use external digestion. By breaking down dead matter they act as decomposers and recycle nutrients.

questions.statement: Euglena is a mixotroph: it can photosynthesize in light but can also feed heterotrophically.
questions.explanation: Euglena has chloroplasts but can also absorb or ingest organic matter, so it can survive in the dark. It is a facultative mixotroph.

questions.text: Many fungi are ___: they secrete enzymes into dead organic matter and absorb the products.
questions.explanation: Fungal hyphae penetrate dead material, release enzymes and absorb the digested molecules across their large surface area.

questions.prompt: Which statement about nutrition in archaea is correct?
options: Different archaea obtain energy from light, from oxidizing inorganic chemicals or from oxidizing organic compounds
All archaea photosynthesize using chlorophyll
All archaea are saprotrophs
Archaea obtain energy only by ingesting other cells
questions.explanation: Archaea are very diverse metabolically: some are chemoautotrophs, some heterotrophs, and some capture light energy (using pigments other than chlorophyll).

questions.prompt: Which group consists of photosynthetic prokaryotes?
options: Fungi
Protozoa
Cyanobacteria
Algae
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria are bacteria with photosynthetic pigments. Algae are photosynthetic too, but they are eukaryotes.

questions.prompt: Paranthropus robustus had very large molars with thick enamel. What does this suggest about its diet?
options: It ate mainly soft fruit
It ate tough, fibrous plant material that needed heavy grinding
It was mainly a meat-eater
It ate only liquids
questions.explanation: Large grinding surfaces and thick enamel resist wear from tough, gritty plant foods, so Paranthropus is interpreted as largely herbivorous.

questions.statement: Homo sapiens has dentition suited to an omnivorous diet.
questions.explanation: Modern humans have incisors for cutting, small canines, and premolars and molars for grinding, suiting a varied diet of plant and animal foods, often cooked.

questions.text: Large, flat ___ with thick enamel are adapted for grinding tough plant material.
questions.explanation: Molars at the back of the jaw have broad surfaces for grinding; incisors cut and canines grip or tear.

questions.prompt: Match each adaptation to its role in herbivory.
questions.explanation: Herbivores and plants exert selection pressures on each other: herbivores evolve ways to feed, plants evolve defences.

questions.prompt: Which is an adaptation of a predator for catching or killing prey?
options: Warning colouration
Toxins stored in the skin
A hard protective shell
Venom injected through fangs to immobilize prey
questions.explanation: Venom is used by predators such as rattlesnakes to subdue prey. The other options help prey animals resist predation.

questions.statement: Bright warning colouration in poisonous prey, such as poison dart frogs, is an adaptation for resisting predation.
questions.explanation: Predators learn to associate the bright colours with toxicity and avoid the prey.

questions.text: Plants that grow on the branches of trees to reach light, without rooting in the soil, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Epiphytes such as many orchids and bromeliads gain light high in the canopy and obtain water from rain and humid air.

questions.prompt: How do lianas harvest light in a forest?
options: They are rooted in the soil and climb up trees to reach the canopy
They grow on branches without any connection to the soil
They are shade-tolerant and stay on the forest floor
They obtain energy from dead organic matter instead of light
questions.explanation: Lianas are woody vines that use trees for support, so they reach the light without investing in a thick trunk.

questions.prompt: Match each plant form to how it obtains light in a forest.

pairs.right: Tall trunks lift leaves into full sunlight
Rooted in soil, climb trees for support
Grow on branches, no roots in soil
Send roots down a host tree and enclose it
Photosynthesize in dim light near the floor

questions.explanation: Light is the key limiting resource in dense forests, so plants have evolved different growth forms to obtain it at different levels.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of predation in order.
questions.explanation: Predators have adaptations for each stage, e.g. keen senses for finding, speed or ambush for catching, and teeth, claws or venom for killing.

options: The niche a species actually occupies in a community
The habitat in which a species evolved
The potential range of conditions and resources a species could use without competition
The smallest area in which a species can survive
questions.explanation: The fundamental niche is set by a species' tolerances and adaptations alone; competition then usually restricts it to a smaller realized niche.

questions.statement: A species' realized niche is usually larger than its fundamental niche.
questions.explanation: The realized niche is part of the fundamental niche: competitors exclude the species from some of the conditions it could otherwise tolerate.

questions.text: The principle that two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely is called competitive ___.
questions.explanation: If niches overlap completely, the better competitor eventually eliminates the other from that niche.

questions.prompt: Gause grew Paramecium aurelia and Paramecium caudatum separately and then together on the same food. What happened when they were grown together?
options: Both reached the same population sizes as when grown alone
P. aurelia outcompeted P. caudatum, which died out
Both species died out
They divided the food evenly and coexisted stably
questions.explanation: Both thrived alone, but together they competed for the same food and P. caudatum was eliminated, demonstrating competitive exclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Actual niche occupied when competitors are present
One species eliminated from a shared niche
No two species in a community share an identical niche

questions.explanation: Competition narrows fundamental niches to realized niches, and complete overlap leads to exclusion, so each species ends up with a unique niche.

questions.statement: Chthamalus barnacles can survive lower on rocky shores, but competition from Balanus restricts their realized niche to the upper shore.
questions.explanation: When Connell removed Balanus, Chthamalus colonized lower rocks, showing that its fundamental niche is larger than its realized niche.

questions.prompt: Two species compete for the same resources in an area. Which outcome is possible?
options: Both species expand into a larger realized niche
The fundamental niches of both species increase
Both species always survive with identical niches
One species is eliminated, or one is restricted to part of its fundamental niche
questions.explanation: Competition either excludes the weaker competitor or forces niche differences, so the species no longer share an identical niche.

questions.prompt: Put the events of competitive exclusion in order.
items: Two species occupy the same niche in an area
They compete for the same limited resources
One species obtains resources slightly more efficiently
Its population increases while the other declines
The less competitive species is eliminated from the area
questions.explanation: Even a small advantage in obtaining shared resources is enough, over many generations, to exclude the weaker competitor.

questions.text: The ___ niche is the range of conditions a species actually occupies in the presence of competitors.
questions.explanation: The realized niche is what we observe in nature; the fundamental niche is revealed only when competitors are absent or removed.

questions.prompt: Why does each species in a stable community have a unique niche?
options: If two species had identical niches, one would outcompete and exclude the other
Each species lives in a different habitat
Niches are assigned randomly to species
Species with the same niche always hybridize
questions.explanation: Competitive exclusion removes complete niche overlap, so coexisting species differ in at least some aspect of their resource use or tolerances.
